title: Do Firms Want to Borrow More? Testing Credit Constraints Using a Directed Lending Program
research_question: Are medium-sized firms in India credit constrained, in the sense that they would profitably expand production if given access to additional working capital at prevailing interest rates? How large is the marginal return to capital for such firms, and to what extent does additional cheap credit substitute for other borrowing rather than finance new production?
data_description: The authors collected firm-level data from loan folders at a major Indian public sector bank, covering 249 borrowing firms with investment in plant and machinery below Rs. 30 million as of 1998, drawn from branches handling business accounts in six major regions including New Delhi and Mumbai. Two waves of data collection (spring 2000 and winter 2002-2003) yielded annual observations from 1996 through 2002, though coverage varies by year (e.g., 175 accounts in 1997, 217 in 1998, 213 in 1999, 124 in 2002). Variables include working capital credit limits granted by the bank, total bank borrowing, interest rates, credit line utilization (turnover/limit), sales revenue, costs, profits, current liabilities, current ratio, projected sales, product description, investment in plant and machinery, date of incorporation, and non-performing-asset status. The unit of observation is firm-year. Values are reported in current rupees.
institutional_context: Indian banks (public and private) are required to direct at least 40% of net credit to a 'priority sector' that includes small-scale industry (SSI); banks failing the target must lend to government agencies at very low rates. In January 1998, the SSI definition was broadened: the ceiling on investment in plant and machinery for priority eligibility was raised from Rs. 6.5 million to Rs. 30 million, making medium-sized firms newly eligible for subsidized priority lending. In January 2000, this expansion was partially reversed: firms with plant and machinery investment between Rs. 10 million and Rs. 30 million lost eligibility. The studied bank is a large public sector bank whose priority-sector share hovered near the 40% target, suggesting the requirement was binding. Bank credit to firms is provided primarily as short-term working capital credit lines with pre-set limits and interest rates a few percentage points above prime, capped at a 4% spread.
